primary_citation.popular_name: Five-Year Rule (Mandatory Dismissal for Failure to Bring to Trial)
primary_citation.original_enactment: Stats. 1984, Ch. 1705 (Trial Court Delay Reduction Act); rule derives from former CCP §583 (at least 1933)
primary_citation.last_amendment: Not amended since 1984 codification. The five-year rule itself unchanged since at least 1933.

five_layer_bar_status.rule: PRESENT — verbatim text captured from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (one sentence, 22 words)
five_layer_bar_status.reasoning: PRESENT — origin context explains why a mandatory trial deadline was needed: cases lingering on dockets indefinitely, witnesses dying, evidence degrading, no hard deadline for prosecution
five_layer_bar_status.historical_loss: PRESENT — documented in historical_chain.md: courts had only discretionary dismissal power, applied inconsistently; cases could sit for decades without resolution, harming defendants, wasting court resources, and producing stale adjudications

evolution_chain.description: Five-year rule existed under former CCP §583 since at least 1933. Recodified as §583.310 by Stats. 1984, Ch. 1705 (Trial Court Delay Reduction Act) without substantive change.
Text unchanged since 1984 codification. Rule unchanged since at least 1933. One sentence, absolute and mandatory.

case_law_documented.case: Hughes v. Board of Architectural Examiners, 17 Cal.4th 763 (1998)
case_law_documented.doctrine: Five-year period is mandatory and jurisdictional -- court loses power

case_law_documented.case: Bruns v. E-Commerce Exchange, Inc., 51 Cal.4th 717 (2011)
case_law_documented.doctrine: Impossibility/impracticability exception is narrow; court congestion insufficient

case_law_documented.case: Sanchez v. City of Los Angeles, 109 Cal.App.4th 1262 (2003)
case_law_documented.doctrine: Court congestion alone does not establish impossibility; plaintiff must show diligence
